steps: At t = 2, the point is (5, 4), dx/dt = 4, and dy/dt = 10, so the slope is 5/2.
For nonzero t, dy/dx = (3t^2 − 2)/(2t) = 3t/2 − 1/t, whose t-derivative is 3/2 + 1/t^2.
Divide that derivative by dx/dt = 2t; at 2 the result is (7/4)/4 = 7/16.

examples.prompt: Determine the convergence interval of Σ from n = 1 to ∞ (x − 2)^n/(n4^n). Justify both endpoints.
steps: The ratio limit in absolute value is |x − 2|/4, so convergence is absolute for |x − 2| < 4 and divergence holds outside.
At x = −2 the series is Σ (−1)^n/n, which converges by the alternating-series test.
At x = 6 it is the harmonic series, which diverges; include only the left endpoint.

examples.prompt: Use the cubic Maclaurin polynomial of e^x to approximate ∫ from 0 to 1/2 e^x dx. Give an error bound using e^x < 2 on this interval.
examples.answer: Approximation = 83/128; error at most 1/1920.
steps: The cubic polynomial is 1 + x + x^2/2 + x^3/6. Its pointwise remainder has magnitude at most 2x^4/24 = x^4/12.
Integrating the polynomial gives 1/2 + 1/8 + 1/48 + 1/384 = 83/128.
Integrating the pointwise bound gives ∫ from 0 to 1/2 x^4/12 dx = (1/2)^5/60 = 1/1920.

worksheets.title: Timed choices with written checks
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Give exact answers. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation. Use 15 minutes for a first pass through items 1–4, then finish the written checks and items 5–6. The total suggested time includes checking; this is not a full examination.

items.prompt: Which expression is an antiderivative of x ln x for x > 0? Select a choice and verify it by differentiation.
steps: Integration by parts with u = ln x and dv = x dx gives (x^2/2)ln x − ∫ x/2 dx.
Differentiating choice B produces x ln x + x/2 − x/2, so the extra terms cancel.
items.skill: Integration by parts and verification

items.prompt: Which statement about Σ from n = 1 to ∞ (−1)^(n−1)/√n is correct? State the test behind your choice.
steps: The magnitudes 1/√n decrease to zero, so the alternating-series test proves convergence.
The absolute-value series is a p-series with p = 1/2 and diverges, so convergence is conditional.
items.skill: Alternation and absolute convergence
choices: It diverges because 1/√n tends to zero.
It converges absolutely by the ratio test.
It diverges because its absolute-value series diverges.
It converges, but its absolute-value series diverges.

items.prompt: For x(t) = e^t and y(t) = e^(2t), what is d^2y/dx^2 at t = 0? Show both differentiation stages.
steps: dy/dx = 2e^(2t)/e^t = 2e^t.
Differentiate this with respect to t and divide by dx/dt again: 2e^t/e^t = 2.
items.skill: Parametric second derivative

items.prompt: Which improper integral has a finite value? Explain why the other three are divergent.
steps: At infinity ∫ x^(−p) converges precisely when p > 1, so C converges and A and B diverge.
Near zero ∫ x^(−p) converges only for p < 1, so the p = 3/2 singularity in D diverges.
items.skill: Improper integral endpoint distinction

items.prompt: For the polar curve r = 2sin θ on 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, set up and evaluate its enclosed area. Explain why the interval traces the region once.
steps: The radius is nonnegative on this interval and the curve travels from the origin around the circle back to the origin without a second traversal.
Area is (1/2)∫ from 0 to π 4sin^2 θ dθ = ∫ from 0 to π (1 − cos 2θ) dθ = π.
items.skill: Polar area and tracing interval

items.prompt: Write the first three nonzero Maclaurin terms for 1/(1 + x^2), then integrate them to approximate ∫ from 0 to 1/2 1/(1 + x^2) dx. Bound the error.
steps: Substitute −x^2 into the geometric series to obtain 1 − x^2 + x^4 − x^6 + ⋯ for |x| < 1.
Integrating the three terms gives 1/2 − 1/24 + 1/160 = 223/480; the integrated series alternates with decreasing terms, and the next magnitude is (1/2)^7/7 = 1/896.
items.skill: Series operations and alternating remainder

worksheets.title: Represent first, compute second
worksheets.directions: Use a graphing calculator where useful. Report decimal answers to three decimal places and retain unrounded intermediate values. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation.

items.prompt: A particle has position (ln(1 + t), t^2/2) meters for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 seconds. Find its velocity at t = 1 and its total distance over the interval.
steps: Differentiate each coordinate to obtain velocity (1/(1 + t), t).
Distance is ∫ from 0 to 2 √(1/(1 + t)^2 + t^2) dt, evaluated numerically.
items.skill: Vector velocity and numerical arc length

items.prompt: Find the area inside r = 2 and outside r = 3cos θ in the angular sector 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2. State where the specified region first appears.
items.answer: It begins at α = arccos(2/3) ≈ 0.841; area ≈ 0.936.
steps: The radial interval 3cos θ ≤ r ≤ 2 exists only when θ ≥ α, since both radii are nonnegative in this sector.
Compute (1/2)∫ from α to π/2 [4 − 9cos^2 θ] dθ ≈ 0.936.
items.skill: Polar intersection and area bounds

items.prompt: Approximate S = Σ from n = 1 to ∞ (−1)^(n−1)/(n 3^n) using four terms. Give a justified interval containing S and determine whether this proves rounding to three decimal places.
items.answer: S4 ≈ 0.287; 0.287037037 ≤ S ≤ 0.287860083. This interval does not justify a unique three-decimal rounding.
steps: The terms decrease to zero; the next term is positive with magnitude 1/(5·3^5) = 1/1215.
S4 = 1/3 − 1/18 + 1/81 − 1/324 = 31/108; add the next magnitude for the upper endpoint. The interval crosses the 0.2875 rounding boundary.
items.skill: Justified approximation versus display precision

items.prompt: Use partial fractions to evaluate ∫ from 0 to 1 1/((x + 1)(x + 3)) dx, then check with numerical integration.
steps: Evaluate (1/2)[ln(x + 1) − ln(x + 3)] between 0 and 1 to obtain (1/2)ln(3/2), matching numerical integration.
items.skill: Partial fractions and numerical check

items.prompt: Let F(x) = ∫ from 0 to x e^(−t^2) dt. Use the first three nonzero terms of its Maclaurin series to estimate F(0.6); compare with numerical integration and bound the truncation error.
items.answer: Series estimate = 0.535776 ≈ 0.536; integral ≈ 0.535; error at most 0.000666515.
steps: Expand e^(−t^2) = 1 − t^2 + t^4/2 − t^6/6 + ⋯ and integrate to get x − x^3/3 + x^5/10.
At 0.6 the polynomial gives 0.535776. The next integrated term has magnitude 0.6^7/42 ≈ 0.000666515 and bounds the alternating remainder; numerical integration gives about 0.535154.
items.skill: Integrated power series and remainder

items.prompt: A proposed antiderivative for √(1 + x^2) is J(x) = [x√(1 + x^2) + ln(x + √(1 + x^2))]/2. Verify J′ and use it to check the arc length of y = x^2/2 on [0, 1].
steps: The derivative of the logarithm is 1/√(1 + x^2); combine it with the derivative of x√(1 + x^2) to obtain √(1 + x^2).
The curve has y′ = x, so its length integrand is √(1 + x^2). Evaluating J(1) − J(0) gives the stated result.
items.skill: Derivative verification and Cartesian length

worksheets.title: Timed written synthesis
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Give exact answers. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation. Allow about 7 minutes per item, then use the remaining time to check domains and hypotheses. These are short written practice tasks, not a full examination.

items.prompt: Determine whether Σ from n = 1 to ∞ n/(n^3 + 4) converges. Explain why knowing only that its terms tend to zero would not settle the question.
items.answer: It converges by limit comparison with Σ 1/n^2.
steps: The ratio [n/(n^3 + 4)]/(1/n^2) = n^3/(n^3 + 4) tends to 1, a finite positive value.
The comparison p-series converges because p = 2; a zero term limit is merely necessary, as the harmonic series shows.
items.skill: Convergence argument and necessary conditions

items.prompt: Let f(x) = Σ from n = 0 to ∞ x^n/(n + 1) for |x| < 1. Find f(0), f′(0), and ∫ from 0 to 1/2 f(x) dx as a convergent series. Explain why your operations are permitted.
steps: Read the constant and linear coefficients from 1 + x/2 + x^2/3 + ⋯.
Termwise integration yields x^(n+1)/(n + 1)^2; the entire interval [0, 1/2] lies strictly inside the convergence radius, where termwise integration is valid.
items.skill: Power-series interpretation and operations

items.prompt: A polar curve is r = 1 + cos θ. At θ = π/2 find its Cartesian point, tangent slope, and equation of the tangent line.
steps: Use x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ; at π/2, r = 1 and r′ = −1.
dx/dθ = r′cos θ − r sin θ = −1 and dy/dθ = r′sin θ + r cos θ = −1, so their ratio is 1.
items.skill: Polar-to-Cartesian tangent

items.prompt: A particle has velocity (2t, 1 − t^2) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 and starts at the origin. Find its displacement vector and total distance exactly.
steps: Integrate each component to get (t^2, t − t^3/3), hence the stated endpoint displacement.
Speed is √(4t^2 + (1 − t^2)^2) = 1 + t^2, so distance is ∫ from 0 to 1 (1 + t^2) dt = 4/3.
items.skill: Vector accumulation and algebraic speed

items.prompt: Let P2 be the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f at 1. Suppose f(1) = 2, f′(1) = −1, f″(1) = 6, and |f‴(x)| ≤ 12 for 1 ≤ x ≤ 3/2. Find P2(3/2) and a guaranteed interval for f(3/2).
steps: The Lagrange bound is 12(1/2)^3/3! = 1/4; add and subtract that bound.
items.skill: Taylor polynomial with interval error

items.prompt: Evaluate ∫ from 1 to ∞ (ln x)/x^2 dx. Show the finite-endpoint calculation before taking a limit, and explain why the logarithm alone does not force divergence.
steps: On [1, b], integration by parts with u = ln x and dv = x^(−2) dx gives 1 − (ln b + 1)/b.
As b → ∞, (ln b)/b and 1/b tend to zero, giving 1. Growth of the denominator compensates for logarithmic growth.
items.skill: Improper integral and integration by parts

weeks.title: Practice examination preparation and error analysis
weeks.objective: Prepare for a separately administered full practice examination, then distinguish conceptual, setup, execution, and justification errors through fresh mathematics and structured corrections.

connection.before: Week 32 combined BC methods in short timed sets.
connection.after: Use identified errors to select targeted repairs in week 34, then demonstrate transfer on fresh tasks.

days: Use sheet A as preparation; write a setup before using any calculator.
Take the separate full practice examination from ap.html#calculus-bc/test/practice-exam under its own section timing and calculator directions; do not substitute these sheets for that document.
After the examination, preserve the first attempt and compare with its separate key. Study this week’s worked corrections.
Use sheet B to audit supplied fictional attempts. For two analogous errors on your own exam, record the first invalid line, corrected rule, and a check.
Complete sheet C as fresh transfer practice. Record whether a correct result is supported by a valid argument rather than remembered from a key.
explanation: A full practice examination is a separate document at ap.html#calculus-bc/test/practice-exam, with its own parts, timing, and calculator rules. These three weekly sheets support preparation and analysis; their lengths and item mix do not reproduce a full exam. Complete a first attempt before opening the separate examination key. Keep unfinished work, since a blank caused by a missing method needs different repair from a nearly complete argument interrupted by time.

An error log is useful only when it identifies a mathematical cause. Record the requested quantity, the first invalid line, the governing rule, and a corrected solution. Distinguish a conceptual error such as treating displacement as distance from a setup error such as reversing inner and outer polar radii. An execution error can occur after a sound setup, and a justification error can leave a correct numerical answer unsupported. A solution may contain more than one type.

Check a repair using a second representation: differentiate an antiderivative, compare a signed integral with geometric area, examine series endpoints individually, or test a proposed general claim with a counterexample. Then solve a fresh problem whose surface features differ. A matching answer on the original problem is weak evidence after viewing its key; a valid argument on a new problem better shows that the repair transfers. Report raw practice points and error patterns, without turning them into a predicted exam score.

examples.prompt: Audit this fictional attempt: for y = ln(1 + x^2), “y′ = 1/(1 + x^2), hence y′(1) = 1/2.” Identify the first invalid line, repair it, and check using symmetry.
examples.answer: The first derivative omitted the inner derivative. y′ = 2x/(1 + x^2), so y′(1) = 1.
steps: The outer logarithm differentiates to the reciprocal of its argument, but the chain rule also needs the derivative 2x of that argument.
Multiply to obtain 2x/(1 + x^2) and substitute x = 1.
The original function is even, so its derivative should be odd; the corrected derivative is odd while the proposed derivative is even.

examples.prompt: Audit the claim “For Σ n!/5^n, the term denominator grows exponentially, so the series converges.” Give a decisive calculation and the missing comparison.
examples.answer: The series diverges; eventually the factorial growth exceeds the fixed-base exponential.
steps: Let a_n = n!/5^n. Then a_(n+1)/a_n = (n + 1)/5.
This ratio tends to infinity and is greater than 1 for all n ≥ 5, so terms eventually grow rather than tend to zero.
The term test already rules out convergence. The phrase “exponential denominator” did not compare it with the numerator.

examples.prompt: A proposed distance for v(t) = cos t on [0, π] is ∫ from 0 to π cos t dt = 0. Diagnose the issue and repair the distance.
examples.answer: Zero is displacement; distance is 2.
steps: Velocity is positive on (0, π/2) and negative on (π/2, π), so a signed integral permits cancellation.
For distance integrate |cos t|: ∫ from 0 to π/2 cos t dt − ∫ from π/2 to π cos t dt.
Each contribution is 1, giving total distance 2 even though final and initial positions coincide.

worksheets.title: Preparation: methods before the full examination
worksheets.directions: Use a graphing calculator where useful. Report decimal answers to three decimal places and retain unrounded intermediate values. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation. This sheet prepares for the separate full practice examination at ap.html#calculus-bc/test/practice-exam. It is not an examination substitute.

items.prompt: Before computing, state a method for lim as x → 0 (e^(2x) − 1 − 2x)/x^2. Evaluate the limit and explain why a coarse decimal table could be misleading.
items.answer: The limit is 2, by series expansion or two applications of l’Hôpital’s rule.
steps: Expand e^(2x) = 1 + 2x + 2x^2 + O(x^3), so cancellation leaves a quotient tending to 2.
Very small x subtracts nearly equal floating-point numbers; that loss of precision can distort a table even when the exact limit exists.
items.skill: Preparation: limit method and calculator limitations

items.prompt: Let F(x) = ∫ from 0 to x (cos t − t/2) dt on [0, 2]. Find the absolute maximum value of F and the x-value where it occurs.
steps: Solve F′(x) = cos x − x/2 = 0 to obtain c ≈ 1.029866529; its derivative −sin x − 1/2 is negative on [0, 2], so this is the only critical point.
F(x) = sin x − x^2/4; compare F(0), F(c), and F(2) to establish the absolute maximum.
items.skill: Preparation: calculator equation and extrema

items.prompt: A vector position is (t − sin t, 1 − cos t), 0 ≤ t ≤ π. Set up a speed integral, simplify its integrand on this interval, and compute distance.
steps: Velocity is (1 − cos t, sin t), giving speed √(2 − 2cos t) = 2sin(t/2) because sin(t/2) ≥ 0 here.
Integrate 2sin(t/2) from 0 to π to obtain [−4cos(t/2)] from 0 to π = 4.
items.skill: Preparation: vector magnitude and sign

items.prompt: For y′ = y(1 − y/10), y(0) = 2, use two Euler steps with h = 0.5 to estimate y(1). Show the updated slope, not only the final decimal.
steps: The initial slope is 2(1 − 2/10) = 1.6, giving y(0.5) ≈ 2.8.
Recompute the slope as 2.8(1 − 2.8/10) = 2.016, then add 0.5(2.016) to get 3.808.
items.skill: Preparation: Euler update

items.prompt: For r = 1 + θ on 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1, write an area integral for the region swept from the origin and compute it. Explain the factor 1/2.
steps: A narrow polar sector has area approximately (1/2)r^2 Δθ, so sum sectors using (1/2)∫ from 0 to 1 (1 + θ)^2 dθ.
The radius is positive and each angle appears once; evaluation gives [(1 + θ)^3/6] from 0 to 1 = 7/6.
items.skill: Preparation: polar area construction

items.prompt: Let f(x) = ln(1 + x). Use its cubic Maclaurin polynomial at x = 0.4. State a justified error bound and compare with the calculator value.
steps: The alternating series gives x − x^2/2 + x^3/3, whose value is 0.4 − 0.08 + 0.064/3.
The next magnitude is 0.4^4/4 = 0.0064; the numerical error about 0.004861 is consistent with that bound.
items.skill: Preparation: series approximation and check

worksheets.title: Structured error analysis of supplied attempts
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Give exact answers. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation. For each supplied attempt, record the first invalid line, the corrected rule, and an independent check. After the separate examination, use the same structure for two errors from your own work; the six supplied tasks stand alone.

items.prompt: Fictional attempt: “If F(x) = ∫ from 0 to sin x (1 + t^2) dt, then F′(x) = 1 + sin^2 x.” Identify the first invalid step, correct F′, and name a point where the omitted factor changes the result.
items.answer: Missing chain factor: F′(x) = (1 + sin^2 x)cos x. At x = π/2 the true derivative is 0, while the attempt gives 2.
steps: The Fundamental Theorem gives the integrand at sin x, but the variable endpoint also contributes its derivative cos x.
Substitution at π/2 makes the discrepancy explicit, identifying a chain-rule setup error rather than arithmetic.
items.skill: Error analysis: chain rule

items.prompt: Fictional attempt: “For x = t^3 and y = t^2 at t = 1, the slope is 3/2.” Correct the slope and tangent line, and identify which ratio was inverted.
steps: The attempt used (dx/dt)/(dy/dt); the needed derivative is dy/dx = (2t)/(3t^2).
At t = 1 this is 2/3 and the point is (1, 1), determining the tangent line.
items.skill: Error analysis: parametric ratio

items.prompt: Fictional attempt: “Σ (x + 1)^n/n^2 has radius 1, so its interval is (−2, 0).” Test both endpoints and repair the conclusion. The sum starts at n = 1.
items.answer: The interval is [−2, 0]; both endpoints converge absolutely.
steps: At x = −2 the terms are (−1)^n/n^2, whose absolute values form a convergent p-series.
At x = 0 the series is Σ 1/n^2, also convergent. The radius only settles the open interior.
items.skill: Error analysis: endpoint omission

items.prompt: Fictional attempt: “∫ from −1 to 1 1/x^2 dx = [−1/x] from −1 to 1 = −2.” Explain the invalid theorem use and determine the actual behavior.
steps: The integrand has an interior singularity at 0, so the Fundamental Theorem cannot be applied across the entire interval as if it were continuous.
Split at 0 and take one-sided limits; even ∫ from ε to 1 x^(−2) dx = 1/ε − 1 diverges as ε → 0+.
items.skill: Error analysis: interior singularity

items.prompt: Fictional attempt: “Since |f‴(0)| = 2, the quadratic Maclaurin error at 1 is at most 2/6.” Explain what information is missing. Give a counterexample with |f‴(0)| = 2 for which the claim fails.
items.answer: A bound throughout [0, 1] is missing. For f(x) = x^3/3 + x^4, P2 = 0 and |f(1) − P2(1)| = 4/3 > 1/3.
steps: A Lagrange bound requires a bound on |f‴(x)| throughout the interval, not only at the center.
Here f‴(x) = 2 + 24x, so the given center value holds but the claimed error bound fails.
items.skill: Error analysis: local value versus interval bound

items.prompt: Fictional attempt: “For y′ = y(1 − y), separate to get dy/[y(1 − y)] = dx. Hence y = 0 and y = 1 are impossible.” Repair the claim, then solve the initial-value problem y(0) = 1.
items.answer: The division omitted equilibrium solutions; y(x) = 1 solves the initial-value problem.
steps: Division by y(1 − y) restricts the algebraic path to y ≠ 0,1 but does not remove solutions from the original equation.
Substituting either constant into the original equation gives derivative zero; y = 1 also satisfies the specified initial condition.
items.skill: Error analysis: division and equilibrium

worksheets.title: Fresh transfer after corrections
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Give exact answers. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation. Complete fresh work without consulting the keys. Afterward, tag each error by its first mathematical cause and identify the calculation in your correction that checks it.

items.prompt: Let G(x) = ∫ from x to x^2 e^(t^2) dt. Find G′(1), and explain how both endpoints contribute.
steps: Differentiate upper and lower endpoint contributions: G′(x) = 2xe^(x^4) − e^(x^2).
At x = 1 this gives 2e − e = e; equal endpoints make G(1) zero but do not make its derivative zero.
items.skill: Transfer: two variable endpoints

items.prompt: For x = 1/t and y = ln t with t > 0, find dy/dx and d^2y/dx^2 at t = 2. Include the change from t-differentiation to x-differentiation.
steps: For general t, dy/dx = (1/t)/(−1/t^2) = −t.
Differentiate −t with respect to t and divide by dx/dt: (−1)/(−1/t^2) = t^2, which is 4 at 2.
items.skill: Transfer: parametric second derivative

items.prompt: Find the convergence interval of Σ from n = 1 to ∞ (2x − 1)^n/n. At which included endpoints, if any, is convergence conditional?
steps: The ratio limit gives |2x − 1| < 1, or 0 < x < 1.
At 0 the alternating harmonic series converges conditionally; at 1 the harmonic series diverges.
items.skill: Transfer: transformed power-series endpoints

items.prompt: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 4 1/√x dx as an improper integral. Contrast its singularity with ∫ from 0 to 4 1/x dx.
items.answer: The first integral is 4; the second diverges.
steps: For ε > 0, ∫ from ε to 4 x^(−1/2) dx = 4 − 2√ε, tending to 4.
The logarithmic antiderivative of 1/x gives ln4 − ln ε → ∞, so a singularity must be tested rather than assumed to cause either outcome.
items.skill: Transfer: convergence at a singular endpoint

items.prompt: The cubic Taylor polynomial of f centered at 2 is P3(x) = 5 + (x − 2)^2 − 2(x − 2)^3. If |f^(4)(x)| ≤ 48 for 2 ≤ x ≤ 5/2, approximate f(5/2) and bound the error.
steps: Substitution gives 5 + 1/4 − 2(1/8) = 5.
The Lagrange remainder is at most 48(1/2)^4/4! = 1/8; the derivative bound applies over the entire required interval.
items.skill: Transfer: Taylor evaluation and bound

items.prompt: A solution of y′ = (y − 2)(3 − y) starts at y(0) = 5/2. Determine the signs of y′ and y″ initially and identify both equilibrium levels. Explain why separation must retain those levels as separate cases.
items.answer: Initially y′ = 1/4 and y″ = 0; equilibria are y = 2 and y = 3.
steps: Differentiate to get y″ = (5 − 2y)y′, which vanishes at y = 5/2 while y′ remains positive.
Both factors vanish at an equilibrium. Dividing by their product during separation excludes those constant cases from that algebra, so they require direct substitution.
items.skill: Transfer: phase-line and second derivative

weeks.title: Targeted repair and fresh reassessment
weeks.objective: Repair specific reasoning failures with explicit checks, then reassess using fresh problems that combine representations and require defended method choices.

connection.before: Week 33 distinguished conceptual, setup, execution, and justification errors.
connection.after: Carry repaired reasoning into an extended investigation of motion, accumulation, and approximation.

days: Select a repair target using an actual incorrect line from prior work; connect it to one of this week’s examples.
Complete sheet A with written rule checks, including items outside the chosen target to detect hidden gaps.
Use sheet B to compare analytic and numerical representations without checking keys mid-task.
Complete sheet C as a fresh reassessment, retaining first attempts.
Compare setup, execution, and justification separately; demonstrate any claimed repair with a correct new calculation from sheet C.
explanation: Targeted repair should change a mathematical decision. If an error involved an absolute value, practice deciding where a sign changes before integrating. If it involved convergence, practice identifying which hypotheses a test needs before naming it. If it involved a derivative, differentiate a composition with its dependency structure visible. A short rule written beside a correctly executed new example is better evidence than a broad promise to be more careful.

A useful repair cycle has three stages. First, reconstruct the failed method using a scaffold that exposes the missing step. Second, choose among methods on a different representation, such as a table instead of a formula. Third, solve a fresh transfer task without that scaffold. This week’s sheets follow those stages. Matching numerical answers are not sufficient when the argument uses an invalid theorem or checks only one endpoint.

Checks must be independent of the mistake they are intended to catch. Repeating the same antiderivative calculation may repeat the same error; differentiating the proposed result is a stronger check. Compare an accumulation result with monotonicity bounds, a distance with displacement magnitude, and a polynomial approximation with a proved remainder estimate. A numerical approximation and a numerical plot can corroborate each other without proving a global claim, so retain an analytic justification when one is requested.

examples.prompt: Repair a sign error in area: find the area between y = x^3 and y = x on [−1, 1] using symmetry and an explicit top-minus-bottom check.
examples.answer: Area = 1/2.
steps: The curves cross at −1, 0, and 1. On (0, 1), x lies above x^3; on (−1, 0), their order reverses.
The geometric areas are equal by origin symmetry, so area is 2∫ from 0 to 1 (x − x^3) dx.
Evaluation gives 2(1/2 − 1/4) = 1/2; the signed integral over [−1, 1] would cancel and is not the requested area.

examples.prompt: Repair a convergence argument for Σ from n = 2 to ∞ 1/[n(ln n)^2] by checking the integral-test hypotheses and evaluating the comparison integral.
examples.answer: The series converges.
steps: For x ≥ 2, f(x) = 1/[x(ln x)^2] is positive and continuous. Its derivative is negative because both x and ln x are positive and increasing.
With u = ln x, ∫ from 2 to b dx/[x(ln x)^2] = 1/ln2 − 1/ln b.
The limit is 1/ln2, finite, so the integral test proves convergence after its hypotheses have been checked.

examples.prompt: For x = t^2 and y = t^4, −1 ≤ t ≤ 1, compare the length of the geometric trace with distance traveled over the whole parameter interval. Set up both integrals.
examples.answer: Trace length = ∫ from 0 to 1 √(1 + 4x^2) dx; traveled distance is twice that value.
steps: Eliminate t to obtain y = x^2 with 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. The motion runs from (1, 1) to (0, 0) and back, so each interior point is traversed twice.
One traversal has Cartesian length ∫ from 0 to 1 √(1 + (2x)^2) dx.
Parametric speed is 2|t|√(1 + 4t^4). Its integral over [−1, 1] equals twice the trace length; the absolute value preserves the reverse traversal.

worksheets.title: Repair with explicit checkpoints
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Give exact answers. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation.

items.prompt: For h(x) = (1 + x^2)^3 sin x, list the outer and inner functions in the first factor. Then find h′(x) and check h′(0) directly using a difference quotient.
steps: The cube is the outer function and 1 + x^2 is its input. Apply the product rule, and the chain rule to the first factor.
Since h(0) = 0, [h(δ) − h(0)]/δ = (1 + δ^2)^3(sin δ/δ) tends to 1 as δ tends to zero.
items.skill: Repair: product and chain structure

items.prompt: To integrate x/(x + 2), first rewrite it as a constant plus a proper fraction. Find an antiderivative and check it by differentiation.
steps: Since x = (x + 2) − 2, the integrand is 1 − 2/(x + 2).
Integrate term by term; differentiation gives 1 − 2/(x + 2) = x/(x + 2).
items.skill: Repair: algebraic preparation

items.prompt: For v(t) = (t − 1)(t − 3) on [0, 4], make a sign chart and find the total distance. Do not integrate across a sign change without explaining it.
steps: Velocity is positive on (0, 1), negative on (1, 3), and positive on (3, 4).
Using V(t) = t^3/3 − 2t^2 + 3t, the signed pieces are 4/3, −4/3, and 4/3. Sum their magnitudes to obtain 4.
items.skill: Repair: sign-controlled total change

items.prompt: Find a quadratic Maclaurin polynomial for f(x) = 1/(2 − x) by computing f(0), f′(0), and f″(0). Compare with the geometric-series expansion.
steps: The three derivative values are 1/2, 1/4, and 1/4; divide the second derivative by 2! for the quadratic coefficient.
Writing f(x) = (1/2)/(1 − x/2) yields the same coefficients, independently checking the factorial.
items.skill: Repair: Taylor coefficient factorial

items.prompt: For Σ from n = 1 to ∞ (−1)^n n/(n + 2), evaluate the term limit before choosing any convergence test. Explain why visible alternation is insufficient.
items.answer: The series diverges because its terms do not tend to zero.
steps: The magnitude n/(n + 2) tends to 1, so the terms oscillate near ±1.
The alternating-series test needs magnitudes tending to zero; that hypothesis fails, and the necessary term condition already proves divergence.
items.skill: Repair: term test before alternation

items.prompt: For r = 3sin θ at θ = π/6, calculate r and r′, then dx/dθ and dy/dθ. Use them to find the tangent slope.
steps: Use x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ; differentiate both products to get r′cos θ − r sin θ and r′sin θ + r cos θ.
At π/6 these become 9/4 − 3/4 and 3√3/4 + 3√3/4; divide the results for the slope.
items.skill: Repair: polar tangent versus radial derivative

worksheets.title: Choose a check from a new representation
worksheets.directions: Use a graphing calculator where useful. Report decimal answers to three decimal places and retain unrounded intermediate values. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation.

items.prompt: A continuously differentiable rate has r(0) = 2, r(1) = 3, r(2) = 5, and r(4) = 9. Estimate ∫ from 0 to 4 r(t) dt using trapezoids, accounting for unequal intervals. Does the table alone tell whether this is an overestimate?
items.answer: Estimate = 20.500. The table alone does not determine the error direction.
steps: Overestimate or underestimate depends on the curve between samples, especially concavity, which is not guaranteed by these values.
items.skill: Repair: unequal spacing and uncertainty

items.prompt: Find all stationary points of f(x) = x^2 e^(−x) on [0, 5] and determine its absolute maximum. Check the result by comparing endpoint values.
items.answer: Stationary points at x = 0 and 2; absolute maximum 4e^(−2) ≈ 0.541 at x = 2.
steps: f′ = xe^(−x)(2 − x), so f increases on (0, 2) and decreases on (2, 5).
Compare f(0) = 0, f(2) ≈ 0.541, and f(5) ≈ 0.168. The endpoint x = 0 has derivative zero, but only 2 is an interior critical candidate.
items.skill: Repair: endpoints and absolute extrema

items.prompt: A parameterized curve has x = t^2 − 1, y = t^3 − 3t for −2 ≤ t ≤ 2. Find all parameter values giving horizontal tangents and report the corresponding points. Check that dx/dt is nonzero there.
steps: Set dy/dt = 3t^2 − 3 = 0, obtaining t = ±1.
dx/dt = 2t is nonzero at both, so each is a horizontal tangent; substitute in both coordinates to distinguish the points.
items.skill: Repair: tangent conditions and parameter values

items.prompt: Estimate ∫ from 0 to 1 cos(x^2) dx with the polynomial 1 − x^4/2 + x^8/24, then find a remainder bound and compare with numerical integration.
steps: Integrate the polynomial to get 1 − 1/10 + 1/216 = 977/1080.
The next integrated magnitude is 1/(6!·13) = 1/9360 and bounds the alternating remainder. Numerical integration is about 0.904524, below the polynomial value about 0.904630.
items.skill: Repair: substitution into a known series

items.prompt: Let y′ = x − y, y(0) = 2. Compare two Euler steps of length 0.5 with the exact value y(1), using the supplied exact solution y = x − 1 + 3e^(−x). State which is larger and verify that the supplied formula solves the differential equation.
items.answer: Euler gives 0.750; exact y(1) = 3/e ≈ 1.104 and is larger.
steps: Slopes at (0, 2) and (0.5, 1) are −2 and −0.5, giving 1 then 0.75.
For the formula, y′ = 1 − 3e^(−x) = x − y and y(0) = 2; substituting x = 1 gives 3/e.
items.skill: Repair: Euler recalculation and exact check

items.prompt: For y = ln x on [1, 3], compare its arc length with the straight-line distance between its endpoints. Write both expressions and explain the inequality.
items.answer: Arc length ≈ 2.302; endpoint distance ≈ 2.282, so the curved distance is larger.
steps: The length is ∫ from 1 to 3 √(1 + 1/x^2) dx; the endpoint distance is √(4 + (ln3)^2).
A curved route is at least as long as its chord, and this curve is not a line segment; numerical evaluations confirm the strict inequality.
items.skill: Repair: distance sanity check

worksheets.title: Fresh reassessment and evidence of repair
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Give exact answers. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation. Finish without the keys. Afterward, choose one earlier error and cite a specific valid step here that shows repair; if no such step is present, solve that task again with the governing rule visible.

items.prompt: A function is defined by f(x) = ax + b for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = x^2 + 1 for x > 1. Find a and b that make it differentiable at 1, and justify why two conditions are needed.
steps: Continuity requires a + b = 2; matching one-sided derivatives requires a = 2.
Combining gives b = 0. A slope match alone would allow a jump and would not establish differentiability.
items.skill: Reassessment: continuity and derivative compatibility

items.prompt: Let A(x) = ∫ from 1 to x ln t dt for x > 0. Determine where A is decreasing, where it is concave up, and its absolute minimum value.
items.answer: A decreases on (0, 1), is concave up on (0, ∞), and has absolute minimum 0 at x = 1.
steps: A′ = ln x is negative below 1 and positive above 1; A″ = 1/x > 0 throughout the domain.
The sign change gives the unique minimum at 1, where equal integration limits give A(1) = 0.
items.skill: Reassessment: accumulation derivative interpretation

items.prompt: Evaluate ∫ from 1 to e (ln x)/x^2 dx. Check the antiderivative by differentiation and state which feature led you to your integration method.
steps: A logarithm times a power suggests parts: choose u = ln x and dv = x^(−2) dx to obtain the antiderivative −(ln x + 1)/x. Differentiating gives (ln x)/x^2.
At e the antiderivative is −2/e and at 1 it is −1; subtract to obtain 1 − 2/e.
items.skill: Reassessment: method selection and verification

items.prompt: For Σ from n = 1 to ∞ (x − 3)^n/(n2^n), determine the interval of convergence and explain why differentiating the series does not preserve every endpoint.
items.answer: Original interval [1, 5); differentiated series converges only on (1, 5).
steps: The ratio test gives |x − 3| < 2; at 1 the alternating harmonic series converges, while at 5 the harmonic series diverges.
The derivative terms are (x − 3)^(n−1)/2^n. At x = 1 their magnitudes are 1/2 and do not tend to zero, so that endpoint is lost.
items.skill: Reassessment: endpoints after operations

items.prompt: For x = 2cos t and y = 2sin t, 0 ≤ t ≤ π, find displacement, distance, and the slope at t = π/4. State one numerical inequality that checks your distance.
items.answer: Displacement = (−4, 0), distance = 2π, slope = −1; 2π > 4 checks that distance exceeds displacement magnitude.
steps: Endpoint subtraction gives (−4, 0); velocity (−2sin t, 2cos t) has constant speed 2, whose integral is 2π.
At π/4, dy/dx = −cot t = −1; the chord length 4 is smaller than the traveled semicircle length.
items.skill: Reassessment: vector geometry and independent check

items.prompt: A student proposes using three terms of Σ from n = 0 to ∞ (−1)^n/(2n + 1) to achieve error below 1/100. Decide if the stated remainder criterion establishes that choice, then find the least number N of terms that the same criterion establishes. Explain the precise inequality you used.
items.answer: Three terms are not justified; the least justified N is 50.
steps: After N terms, the next magnitude is 1/(2N + 1). For N = 3 the bound is 1/7, which is too large.
Require 1/(2N + 1) < 1/100, so 2N + 1 > 100 and the least integer is 50. The criterion is sufficient, not a claim about the exact minimum error.
items.skill: Reassessment: strict inequality and error justification

weeks.title: Investigation: motion, accumulation, and approximation
weeks.objective: Build and audit a self-contained planar-motion model that converts deposition per distance into accumulation per time, compares numerical approximations, and establishes a material-budget decision.

connection.before: Week 34 checked repaired methods with fresh representations and independent calculations.
connection.after: Week 36 critiques a new model dossier and explores explicitly labeled extensions of these ideas.

days: Read the supplied inspection-path brief and identify quantities, units, and assumptions.
Use sheet A to derive motion and accumulation expressions before any numerical computation.
Use sheet B to compare numerical methods, track rounding, and test data limitations.
Use sheet C to establish approximation bounds and make a justified material-budget decision.
Write the technical recommendation in the final task, separating the idealized model conclusion from uncertainty in real operation.
explanation: This original paper investigation supplies its complete path, deposition rule, time interval, and assumptions in the Inspection-path brief. A position (x(t), y(t)) gives velocity (x′(t), y′(t)); speed is the magnitude of that vector. If coating mass is specified per meter traveled, multiply that quantity by meters per second to obtain grams per second. Integrating concentration alone over time would have units of gram-seconds per meter and would answer the wrong question.

The model produces both elementary and non-elementary expressions. Coordinate displacements follow from endpoint subtraction or component integration, while total distance requires integrating speed. A graphing calculator can approximate the speed integral, and a table supports trapezoidal or midpoint estimates. Those computations should agree within their errors, not necessarily digit for digit. Decide which source of error is being discussed: truncating a polynomial, replacing a curve by line segments, rounding the displayed data, or simplifying the physical model.

A budget decision close to a threshold needs a bound, not merely two rounded decimals that look equal. For f(u) = √(1 + u) with u ≥ 0, Taylor’s theorem gives f(u) = 1 + u/2 − u^2/8 + R, where 0 ≤ R ≤ u^3/16 because f‴(u) = 3/[8(1 + u)^(5/2)] is positive and at most 3/8. Substitute u = t^2, multiply the resulting inequality by the positive deposition-per-distance factor, and integrate. This turns a local approximation into a justified interval for total deposited mass. The bound establishes the stated mathematical model; it does not justify the unmeasured behavior of a real machine.

examples.prompt: A demonstration robot follows x(t) = 2t and y(t) = t^2, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Write its displacement vector, speed, and distance integral, distinguishing all three quantities.
examples.answer: Displacement = (2, 1); speed = 2√(1 + t^2); distance = ∫ from 0 to 1 2√(1 + t^2) dt.
steps: Endpoint subtraction yields (x(1) − x(0), y(1) − y(0)) = (2, 1).
Differentiate to get velocity (2, 2t), whose magnitude is √(4 + 4t^2).
Integrate speed for distance; the displacement magnitude √5 describes the chord and does not replace the curved-path integral.

examples.prompt: A separate straight-path applicator moves at speed 1 + t meters per second for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. Its deposition density is 4 grams per meter. Find the mass used and verify its units.
examples.answer: 16 grams.
steps: Multiply density by speed: the time rate is 4(1 + t) g/s because (g/m)(m/s) = g/s.
Integrate from 0 to 2: 4[t + t^2/2] from 0 to 2 = 16.
The distance is ∫ from 0 to 2 (1 + t) dt = 4 m, and 4 g/m times 4 m independently confirms 16 g.

examples.prompt: Approximate √1.1 with the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f(u) = √(1 + u) at u = 0, and use 0 < f‴(u) ≤ 3/8 on [0, 0.1] to bound the error and its sign.
examples.answer: Approximation = 1.04875; the true value is larger by at most 1/16000 = 0.0000625.
steps: The coefficients f(0) = 1, f′(0) = 1/2, and f″(0) = −1/4 give P2(u) = 1 + u/2 − u^2/8.
The Lagrange remainder is f‴(ξ)(0.1)^3/6, positive and at most (3/8)(0.1)^3/6 = 1/16000.

passages.title: Inspection-path brief: a supplied mathematical model
passages.text:
An idealized applicator follows x(t) = t meters and y(t) = t^2/2 meters for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1/2 second. Its start is (0, 0). Positive x is right and positive y is up. At time t, it deposits coating at density c(t) = 2 + t^2 grams per meter of path traveled. Assume continuous motion, no loss, no overlap, and no delay in the deposition rule. It starts with 3 grams of coating. The permitted mass used during this run is 1.085 grams. This is a designed mathematical scenario, not measured operational data.

For computations define s(t) = √(1 + t^2) and Q(t) = (2 + t^2)√(1 + t^2). A controller tabulates the following rounded values; the analytic formulas remain authoritative.
| t (s) | 0 | 0.125 | 0.250 | 0.375 | 0.500 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| s(t) (m/s) | 1.000000 | 1.007782 | 1.030776 | 1.068000 | 1.118034 |
| Q(t) (g/s) | 2.000000 | 2.031311 | 2.125976 | 2.286189 | 2.515576 |

Each tabulated value is rounded to the nearest 0.000001 in its stated unit. The mass used is the time integral of Q. Use exact expressions or at least six decimal places when comparing justified bounds with the 1.085-gram budget. Final ordinary calculator answers use three decimals; retain additional digits when the task concerns error or a threshold.

figures.alt: Coordinate plot of the supplied path x = t, y = t squared divided by 2, from (0, 0) to (0.5, 0.125), with an arrow toward increasing t. Axes are in meters.
figures.caption: Inspection path; the coordinate axes have different displayed scales.

worksheets.title: Derive the investigation model
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Give exact answers. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation.

items.prompt: From the Inspection-path brief, derive velocity and acceleration vectors. Evaluate each at the end of the run and state the units.
items.answer: v(t) = (1, t) m/s and a(t) = (0, 1) m/s^2; at t = 1/2 they are (1, 1/2) and (0, 1).
steps: Differentiate the two position coordinates once for velocity and again for acceleration.
Substitute t = 1/2 and retain vector components; acceleration is not the same quantity as speed.
items.skill: Investigation: vector model derivation

items.prompt: Find the endpoint displacement and its magnitude. Then write the exact integral for distance traveled and give a reason the distance exceeds the displacement magnitude.
items.answer: Displacement = (1/2, 1/8) m; magnitude = √17/8 m; distance = ∫ from 0 to 1/2 √(1 + t^2) dt and is larger.
steps: Evaluate the endpoint coordinates and use the Pythagorean theorem for their straight-line separation.
The velocity magnitude is √(1 + t^2); integrating it follows the curved path, which is not a straight segment.
items.skill: Investigation: displacement versus traveled length

items.prompt: Starting with deposition density c, derive the time rate of coating use. Write a formula for remaining coating M(t) and find M′(t), including its sign and units.
items.answer: Q(t) = (2 + t^2)√(1 + t^2) g/s; M(t) = 3 − ∫ from 0 to t Q(u) du g; M′(t) = −Q(t) < 0 g/s.
steps: Multiply grams per meter by speed in meters per second to obtain Q.
Subtract accumulated use from the initial 3 grams; the Fundamental Theorem gives the negative rate because Q is positive.
items.skill: Investigation: unit conversion and accumulation

items.prompt: Find the slope dy/dx at the end of the path and write the tangent-line equation there. Explain why dy/dt alone happens to have the same numerical value as dy/dx in this model.
steps: The parametric slope is (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = t/1, so its ending value is 1/2.
The equality of the numerical values occurs because dx/dt = 1; it is not a general replacement for the parametric slope rule.
items.skill: Investigation: path geometry

items.prompt: Prove that speed increases for 0 < t ≤ 1/2 and find its minimum and maximum. Use them to bound distance without evaluating its integral.
items.answer: Speed rises from 1 to √5/2 m/s; 1/2 ≤ distance ≤ √5/4 m.
steps: On a time interval of length 1/2, multiply the minimum and maximum speeds by 1/2 to bound the integral.
items.skill: Investigation: monotonicity bounds

items.prompt: Is deposition faster per unit time at the end or at the start? Prove your conclusion by differentiating Q, then give its exact endpoint rates.
items.answer: Q increases; Q(0) = 2 g/s and Q(1/2) = 9√5/8 g/s.
steps: The product rule gives Q′ = 2t√(1 + t^2) + t(2 + t^2)/√(1 + t^2) = t(4 + 3t^2)/√(1 + t^2).
This is positive for t > 0. Substitution gives 2 and (9/4)(√5/2), respectively.
items.skill: Investigation: rate monotonicity

worksheets.title: Compare numerical evidence
worksheets.directions: Use a graphing calculator where useful. Report decimal answers to three decimal places and retain unrounded intermediate values. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation.

items.prompt: Use the supplied speed table and all four subintervals to estimate distance by the trapezoidal rule. Show the weighted sum and compare with numerical integration of the analytic formula.
items.answer: Table trapezoid ≈ 0.520697 m, or 0.521 m to three decimals; analytic integral ≈ 0.520114 m, or 0.520 m to three decimals.
steps: Average the endpoint speeds: E = (1.000000 + 1.118034)/2 = 1.059017.
Add the three interior speeds: I = 1.007782 + 1.030776 + 1.068000 = 3.106558.
The trapezoid sum is 0.125(E + I) = 0.520696875. The analytic integral is about 0.520114410; retain unrounded values for comparison.
items.skill: Investigation: trapezoidal distance

items.prompt: Use two midpoint rectangles on [0, 1/2] to estimate mass used from the Q table. Compare this estimate with numerical integration and report the signed error.
items.answer: Midpoint ≈ 1.079375 g; integral ≈ 1.084893 g; signed error ≈ −0.005518 g.
steps: Each rectangle has width 0.25 and uses midpoint 0.125 or 0.375: 0.25(2.031311 + 2.286189) = 1.079375.
Numerically integrate (2 + t^2)√(1 + t^2); subtract its value about 1.084893028 from the midpoint estimate.
items.skill: Investigation: midpoint accumulation

items.prompt: Estimate coating remaining at the end using all four trapezoids from the Q table. Compare the resulting used-mass estimate with the budget, and explain why this estimate alone does not settle the true model decision.
items.answer: Trapezoid use ≈ 1.087658 g, leaving ≈ 1.912342 g. The estimate exceeds 1.085 g but alone does not prove the true integral exceeds it.
steps: Average the endpoint rates: E = (2.000000 + 2.515576)/2 = 2.257788.
Subtract from 3 for remaining mass. An approximation above a threshold can arise from positive approximation error; an error bound or better analysis is needed.
items.skill: Investigation: estimate versus decision

items.prompt: Find the time when half of the total coating used in the run has been deposited. Give the integral equation, solve it numerically, and compare the time with 0.25 s.
steps: Solve ∫ from 0 to T Q(t) dt = (1/2)∫ from 0 to 1/2 Q(t) dt; Q > 0 ensures a unique solution.
Numerical solution is about 0.265 s. Since Q increases, the first half of the time deposits less than half the mass.
items.skill: Investigation: inverse accumulation

items.prompt: Compute average speed and average mass-use rate over the run. Then compute total mass divided by total distance. Explain why that last ratio has a different unit and meaning.
items.answer: Average speed ≈ 1.040 m/s; average mass-use rate ≈ 2.170 g/s; mass/distance ≈ 2.086 g/m.
steps: Divide each time integral by the duration 0.5 s to obtain the first two averages.
Divide mass about 1.084893028 g by distance about 0.520114410 m for about 2.085874 g/m; this is the distance-weighted average deposition density.
items.skill: Investigation: three distinct averages

items.prompt: Each Q-table value is rounded to six decimal places. Bound the error in the four-panel trapezoidal sum due solely to this rounding. Can rounding explain the difference between that sum and the analytic integral?
items.answer: Rounding contributes at most 0.00000025 g, far below the roughly 0.002765 g discrepancy; discretization dominates.
steps: Each listed rate has error at most 0.0000005 g/s. The positive trapezoidal weights add to the duration 0.5 s.
Thus the weighted error is at most 0.5(0.0000005) = 0.00000025 g, which cannot explain the observed discrepancy.
items.skill: Investigation: numerical error sources

worksheets.title: Justify and communicate the model decision
worksheets.directions: Use a graphing calculator where useful. Report decimal answers to three decimal places and retain unrounded intermediate values. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation. Use the supplied brief with every item. Show exact expressions or at least six decimal places for error bounds and budget comparisons; ordinary final measurements may be rounded to three decimals.

items.prompt: For 0 ≤ t ≤ 1/2, Taylor’s theorem gives 0 ≤ √(1 + t^2) − p(t) ≤ t^6/16, where p(t) = 1 + t^2/2 − t^4/8. Integrate p from 0 to 1/2, and give a one-sided interval guaranteed to contain the true path length.
steps: The speed inequality is 0 ≤ s(t) − p(t) ≤ t^6/16. The polynomial integral is 1/2 + 1/48 − 1/1280 = 1997/3840.
Integrating the upper error bound gives (1/2)^7/(16·7) = 1/14336; add it only to the upper endpoint.
items.skill: Investigation: justified length

items.prompt: Construct q(t) = (2 + t^2)p(t), expand it, and integrate it to approximate total mass used. Retain at least six decimal places for later comparison.
steps: Multiply the two polynomials, combining their t^2 and t^4 terms carefully.
Integrate each term over [0, 1/2]; the last term contributes −(1/2)^7/56 = −1/7168.
items.skill: Investigation: approximation of a product

items.prompt: Use 2 + t^2 ≤ 9/4 and the error bound for p to bound the difference between true mass and the q-integral from item 2. Give the sign and an explicit numerical upper bound.
steps: Multiply 0 ≤ s − p ≤ t^6/16 by the nonnegative factor 2 + t^2, then bound that factor by 9/4.
Integrate (9/64)t^6 from 0 to 1/2 to obtain 9/57344, preserving the one-sided sign.
items.skill: Investigation: propagated error bound

items.prompt: Use a justified interval, not only a calculator decimal, to decide whether the model stays within the 1.085-gram budget. State a guaranteed lower bound on unused budget.
items.answer: Yes. Model use is at most about 1.084913272 g, leaving at least about 0.000086728 g of the budget.
steps: Add the bound 9/57344 to the exact q-integral to obtain an upper bound less than 1.085.
Subtract that upper bound from 1.085. Both true use and the budget round to 1.085 g at three decimals, so the additional digits and bound are essential.
items.skill: Investigation: threshold justification

items.prompt: A modified controller changes only the density rule to c_new(t) = (1 + ε)(2 + t^2), ε ≥ 0. Use the justified upper mass bound to find a sufficient upper limit on ε that still establishes the budget. State why the limit is sufficient rather than exact.
steps: The new mass is (1 + ε) times the original mass, hence is at most (1 + ε)U.
Solve (1 + ε)U ≤ 1.085. Since U may exceed the true mass, the resulting allowable ε is conservative.
items.skill: Investigation: sensitivity and conservative bounds

items.prompt: Write a short technical recommendation using at least two quantitative results from this investigation. Address the budget, why the trapezoid result and the justified conclusion differ, and one assumption whose failure could invalidate the operational interpretation.
items.answer: Sample: Under the supplied model the run uses at most 1.084913272 g, below 1.085 g. The 1.087658 g trapezoid estimate is coarser and cannot overturn the bound. Loss, delayed deposition, or a changed path could alter actual use; the mathematical margin is only about 0.000086728 g guaranteed.
steps: Use the justified upper bound for the decision and cite the explicit trapezoidal approximation as an estimate with discretization error.
Name an assumption from the brief and connect its failure to a changed rate or accumulated mass; do not claim real-world calibration from designed data.
items.skill: Investigation: evidence-based model communication

weeks.title: Capstone, mathematical critique, and further study
weeks.objective: Critique a supplied mathematical model with complete evidence, synthesize motion and accumulation, and distinguish course conclusions from clearly labeled enrichment in reparameterization and optimal timing.

connection.before: Week 35 justified an accumulation decision using Taylor bounds and unit analysis.
connection.after: Further study can develop rigorous approximation, multivariable motion, and variational optimization; the labeled enrichment is exploratory, not an additional exam requirement.

days: Read the elliptical-transfer dossier and identify what each disputed claim is actually measuring.
Use sheet A to audit the four claims with exact calculations.
Use sheet B to compare numerical estimates and a changed timing schedule.
Explore sheet C’s explicitly labeled enrichment after completing the core critique.
Assemble a concise capstone report whose conclusions cite computations, identify assumptions, and distinguish model results from further-study questions.
explanation: A mathematical critique evaluates a claim against its definitions and evidence. The supplied dossier contains deliberately disputed claims; none should be accepted merely because it appears in a technical memo. Displacement is an endpoint vector, distance integrates speed, acceleration is a vector derivative, and energy accumulates a stated power rule. Each quantity has its own units. A correct critique replaces an invalid statement with a checkable result rather than only labeling it wrong.

Two motions can follow the same geometric path at different rates. Coordinate elimination identifies the path, while time derivatives describe how it is traversed. A change of parameter that preserves orientation can preserve geometric length even though velocity, acceleration, duration, and energy use change. When the consumption rule includes both a baseline rate and a speed-dependent term, slowing down reduces one contribution while increasing the time over which the baseline is paid.

The core capstone uses derivatives, integrals, vector magnitude, numerical sums, and justified comparisons already studied. Sheet C labels enrichment explicitly: it derives a general speed-change identity, examines reparameterization, and optimizes a constant time-scaling factor. These are applications toward further study, not claims of additional required exam content. A model optimum is conditional on the stated family of timing schedules and power law; it is not an optimum among every possible real-world motion.

examples.prompt: A particle moves on x = 3cos t, y = 3sin t for 0 ≤ t ≤ π/2. Find displacement, distance, and their magnitudes’ relationship.
examples.answer: Displacement = (−3, 3); its magnitude is 3√2. Distance = 3π/2 > 3√2.
steps: The initial and final positions are (3, 0) and (0, 3), so subtracting gives the displacement.
Velocity is (−3sin t, 3cos t) and has constant speed 3, so the speed integral is 3π/2.
The arc is longer than its chord. Constant speed does not make a curved path into a straight displacement.

examples.prompt: In a separate one-dimensional model, a machine moves 4 meters at constant speed k meters per second and consumes power 2 + k^2 watts. Express its energy use and find the minimizing positive k.
examples.answer: Energy E(k) = 8/k + 4k joules; minimum at k = √2 m/s, with E = 8√2 J.
steps: The duration is distance divided by speed, 4/k seconds, so energy is (2 + k^2)(4/k).
Differentiate to get E′ = −8/k^2 + 4. The only positive critical point is √2.
E′ is negative below √2 and positive above, so it is the global minimum within the stated constant-speed family.

examples.prompt: For v(t) = (1, 2t), compute the derivative of speed directly and compare it with the acceleration magnitude at t = 1.
examples.answer: Speed derivative is 4t/√(1 + 4t^2), giving 4/√5 at 1; acceleration magnitude is 2.
steps: Speed is √(1 + 4t^2), so differentiation gives 4t/√(1 + 4t^2).
Acceleration is v′ = (0, 2), with magnitude 2.
At t = 1 these quantities differ: acceleration can change velocity direction as well as its magnitude.

passages.title: Elliptical-transfer dossier and disputed memo
passages.text:
A designed transfer mechanism follows x(t) = 2cos t meters and y(t) = sin t meters for 0 ≤ t ≤ π/2 seconds. Positive x is right and positive y is up. The trigonometric arguments use radians; time is measured in seconds with a numerical angular rate of 1 radian per second. Let s(t) be its speed in meters per second. Its idealized power law is P(t) = 1 + s(t)^2 watts when the numerical speed is entered in meters per second; equivalently, P = P0 + κs^2 with P0 = 1 W and κ = 1 J·s/m^2. Energy use is the time integral of P. Ignore friction changes, startup transients, and mechanical speed limits.

A fictional memo makes four disputed claims: (i) total distance is √5 meters because the endpoints are (2, 0) and (0, 1); (ii) speed equals the magnitude of acceleration at every time; (iii) energy use is P(0) times the duration; (iv) any new clock schedule following the same quarter ellipse uses the same energy. These statements are claims to audit, not supplied facts.

For a comparison schedule, a positive scale k gives X(u) = 2cos(ku), Y(u) = sin(ku), on 0 ≤ u ≤ π/(2k) seconds. Apply the same power law using this schedule’s actual speed. All data needed for the investigation are given here. The tasks on sheet C labeled Enrichment go beyond the required synthesis into general identities and model optimization.

figures.alt: First-quadrant quarter ellipse from (2, 0) to (0, 1), with arrow pointing from the positive x axis toward the positive y axis. A dashed segment joins the endpoints. Both axes measure meters.
figures.caption: The curved path and its straight endpoint chord.

worksheets.title: Core capstone: audit the memo
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Give exact answers. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation.

items.prompt: Eliminate t to find the Cartesian path equation and its quadrant restriction. Explain which information about the motion the Cartesian equation loses.
items.answer: x^2/4 + y^2 = 1, with x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. The equation loses the timing and orientation unless those are separately stated.
steps: Substitute cos t = x/2 and sin t = y into cos^2 t + sin^2 t = 1.
The parameter interval confines the path to the first quadrant and traverses from (2, 0) to (0, 1), facts not encoded by the full ellipse equation alone.
items.skill: Capstone: path versus parameterization

items.prompt: Audit memo claim (i). Find the displacement vector and its magnitude, then give a correct expression for total distance and explain the strict inequality between the two lengths.
items.answer: Displacement = (−2, 1) m; magnitude = √5 m. Distance L = ∫ from 0 to π/2 √(1 + 3sin^2 t) dt > √5 m.
steps: Differentiate the coordinates to obtain velocity (−2sin t, cos t), whose magnitude is √(4sin^2 t + cos^2 t).
The memo calculated the chord. The traversed quarter ellipse is not a straight line segment, so its length is strictly larger.
items.skill: Capstone: displacement claim

items.prompt: Audit memo claim (ii) using t = 0 as a counterexample. Then find every time in [0, π/2] when the numerical speed and acceleration magnitude are equal.
items.answer: At t = 0, speed is 1 m/s and acceleration magnitude is 2 m/s^2; their numerical values coincide only at t = π/4. The units are different quantities regardless.
steps: Acceleration is (−2cos t, −sin t), whose squared magnitude is 4cos^2 t + sin^2 t.
Equate numerical squares 1 + 3sin^2 t = 4 − 3sin^2 t to get sin^2 t = 1/2, hence t = π/4 in the given interval.
items.skill: Capstone: counterexample and units

items.prompt: Audit memo claim (iii). Derive P(t), integrate it exactly, and compute the memo’s constant-rate estimate for comparison.
items.answer: P(t) = 2 + 3sin^2 t W; true energy = 7π/4 J, while the memo gives π J.
steps: The squared speed is 1 + 3sin^2 t; adding the baseline gives the stated power.
Integrate over [0, π/2]: 2(π/2) + 3(π/4) = 7π/4. The initial power is only 2 W, so its duration product is π.
items.skill: Capstone: variable rate accumulation

items.prompt: Find minimum and maximum power and use them to bound the true energy. Does the exact value from your own calculation satisfy the bounds?
items.answer: 2 ≤ P ≤ 5 W, hence π ≤ energy ≤ 5π/2 J. The value 7π/4 lies between them.
steps: sin^2 t ranges from 0 to 1, so the stated power bounds follow from P = 2 + 3sin^2 t.
Multiply by duration π/2; comparing coefficients 1 ≤ 7/4 ≤ 5/2 verifies consistency.
items.skill: Capstone: integral bounds

items.prompt: Use derivatives to decide whether speed is increasing, decreasing, or constant in the interior of the interval. Explain why neither a fixed path nor a fixed angular rate guarantees constant speed.
steps: For s = √(1 + 3sin^2 t), s′ = 3sin t cos t/√(1 + 3sin^2 t), positive in the open first quadrant.
The unequal ellipse axis lengths make equal parameter increments cover different arc lengths; fixed angular parameter rate does not imply fixed speed.
items.skill: Capstone: speed variation

worksheets.title: Core capstone: quantitative comparisons
worksheets.directions: Use a graphing calculator where useful. Report decimal answers to three decimal places and retain unrounded intermediate values. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation.

items.prompt: Evaluate the true path length numerically and compare it with the memo’s chord estimate. Report the absolute discrepancy and the discrepancy as a percentage of the true length.
items.answer: L ≈ 2.422 m; chord ≈ 2.236 m; discrepancy ≈ 0.186 m or 7.681% of true length.
steps: Numerically integrate √(1 + 3sin^2 t) over [0, π/2] to obtain about 2.422112055.
Subtract √5 and divide by the unrounded length, then multiply by 100 for the percentage.
items.skill: Capstone: quantitative critique

items.prompt: Approximate path length using four trapezoids with nodes 0, π/8, π/4, 3π/8, π/2. Compare with numerical integration. Does a close decimal match alone establish the rule’s error sign on every partition?
items.answer: Trapezoid ≈ 2.422 m, about 2.422103098 before rounding; its error is about −0.000008957 m. A close match does not establish a universal error sign.
steps: Compute each speed from its formula and multiply the endpoint-half-weighted sum by π/8.
Compare with the integral; the speed’s concavity changes, so this single comparison is evidence for this partition, not a proof for all partitions.
items.skill: Capstone: quadrature evidence and limits

items.prompt: Find the time when power first reaches 4 W and the fraction of the total energy used by that time. Write the equation and accumulated-energy expression.
steps: Solve 2 + 3sin^2 T = 4, giving T = arcsin√(2/3) ≈ 0.955316618.
Accumulated energy is (7/2)T − (3/4)sin2T; divide this by 7π/4 to obtain about 0.480.
items.skill: Capstone: rate threshold and accumulated fraction

items.prompt: For the comparison schedule with k = 2, find duration, initial and final speeds, and total distance. Explain which result is unchanged and why.
items.answer: Duration ≈ 0.785 s; initial speed = 2.000 m/s, final speed = 4.000 m/s; distance ≈ 2.422 m.
steps: Differentiation gives speed 2√(1 + 3sin^2(2u)); duration is π/4.
Substitute t = 2u in its length integral; the factor 2 cancels du = dt/2, leaving the original path length.
items.skill: Capstone: changed clock and geometric length

items.prompt: For k = 2, apply the actual speed to the power law and compute energy. Compare with the original run, and decide memo claim (iv) using this counterexample.
items.answer: New energy = 11π/4 ≈ 8.639 J versus 7π/4 ≈ 5.498 J; claim (iv) is false.
steps: The new power is 1 + 4(1 + 3sin^2(2u)). Integrate from 0 to π/4.
Substitution gives π/4 + 2∫ from 0 to π/2 (1 + 3sin^2 t) dt = π/4 + 5π/2 = 11π/4, despite unchanged distance.
items.skill: Capstone: path-invariant versus rate-dependent quantities

items.prompt: Prepare a replacement memo of 120–180 words that corrects all four claims using quantitative evidence. Include one limitation of the power model and distinguish exact values from numerical approximations.
items.answer: A defensible memo identifies √5 as displacement magnitude, gives L ≈ 2.422 m, refutes speed–acceleration equality with the t = 0 values, gives exact energy 7π/4 J, and uses k = 2 energy 11π/4 J to refute timing invariance. It names an ignored effect such as startup transients as a model limitation.
steps: Organize the response around the four original claims and attach a calculation or counterexample to each correction.
Label approximate length and exact energies explicitly, and explain how the chosen unmodeled effect could change the power law or timing. Wording need not match the sample.
items.skill: Capstone: mathematical communication

worksheets.title: Enrichment: identities, timing, and further study
worksheets.directions: No calculator. Give exact answers. All angles are in radians. Show reasoning, include units where given, and distinguish an exact result from an approximation. All six tasks on this sheet are explicitly labeled enrichment for further study. They are not additional claims about required exam content. Show exact answers and justify the domain of each conclusion.

items.prompt: Enrichment. For a differentiable velocity v = (a(t), b(t)) with positive speed s, derive s′ = (v · v′)/s, where v · v′ means aa′ + bb′. Apply the identity to the dossier’s original velocity and recover its speed derivative.
items.answer: s′ = (aa′ + bb′)/√(a^2 + b^2); in the model, s′ = 3sin t cos t/√(1 + 3sin^2 t).
steps: Differentiate s = (a^2 + b^2)^(1/2) using the chain rule and cancel the factor 2.
For v = (−2sin t, cos t), its dot product with acceleration is 4sin t cos t − sin t cos t = 3sin t cos t.
items.skill: Enrichment: general speed-change identity

items.prompt: Enrichment. For any k > 0 in the dossier’s timing family, prove that total distance is independent of k. State which sign or orientation assumption your substitution uses.
items.answer: The distance is always L = ∫ from 0 to π/2 √(1 + 3sin^2 t) dt.
steps: The new speed is k√(1 + 3sin^2(ku)) because k is positive.
Use t = ku with du = dt/k; endpoints become 0 and π/2 and the factors cancel. Positivity preserves the forward orientation.
items.skill: Enrichment: reparameterization invariance

items.prompt: Enrichment. Derive the total energy E(k) for the entire positive timing family without numerical integration. Separate the baseline and speed-dependent contributions.
steps: Baseline power 1 W over duration π/(2k) contributes π/(2k).
The speed-squared contribution is ∫ k^2(1 + 3sin^2(ku)) du; substitution t = ku gives k(π/2 + 3π/4) = 5πk/4.
items.skill: Enrichment: parameter-dependent accumulation

items.prompt: Enrichment. Find the positive value of k minimizing E(k) in this timing family and its exact minimum energy. Justify global minimality rather than only solving E′ = 0.
steps: E′(k) = −π/(2k^2) + 5π/4 vanishes when k^2 = 2/5.
The derivative is negative below this positive value and positive above; E also grows without bound as k approaches zero or infinity. Substitution gives π√(5/2).
items.skill: Enrichment: optimization with domain

items.prompt: Enrichment. Use your formula for E(k) to decide whether making k arbitrarily small can make energy arbitrarily close to zero. Explain the competing mathematical mechanisms and how the conclusion depends on the baseline term.
items.answer: No. E(k) → ∞ as k → 0+ because π/(2k) grows without bound, even though 5πk/4 tends to zero. Without baseline power, this model’s energy would tend to zero.
steps: Separate the two positive contributions and take their limits individually.
The fixed nonzero baseline is paid for an increasingly long time; removing it changes the model and removes the balancing mechanism.
items.skill: Enrichment: asymptotics and model assumptions

items.prompt: Enrichment and capstone reflection. A new memo says the minimizing k proves the best possible timing schedule on the ellipse. Assess the scope of that statement. Give one precise broader mathematical question that the calculation has not answered and one condition under which your result remains valid.
items.answer: The calculation optimizes only constant scale k > 0 within the specified power model. It does not compare arbitrary time-varying schedules. A broader question is whether a nonconstant angular rate lowers energy while following the same path. The derived optimum remains valid among constant scale schedules with the stated baseline, quadratic speed law, and no speed limits.
steps: Identify the domain of optimization: one positive constant k, not every possible function describing timing.
Formulate a new question outside that domain and state the assumptions retained by the proved result; distinguish this next research step from an established conclusion.
items.skill: Enrichment: scope of an optimization claim
